chief_complaint: sudden severe prolonged fetal heart rate bradycardia immediately following artificial rupture of membranes
hpi_details: 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks experiencing abrupt fetal bradycardia down to 70 bpm after amniotomy where vaginal examination palpates a pulsating loop of umbilical cord protruding through the cervix requiring elevation of fetal presenting part and immediate STAT Cesarean delivery.
ideas: thinks this is related to cord prolapse acute obstetric emergency
concerns: worried about serious complications and prolonged recovery
expectations: wants diagnostic certainty and immediate evidence-based management

clinical_knowledge.topic: Umbilical cord prolapse evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Umbilical cord prolapse is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: An abrupt, persistent fetal bradycardia or recurrent variable decelerations immediately after membrane rupture should prompt immediate assessment for cord prolapse.
A pulsating umbilical cord palpated below the presenting part or seen at the introitus confirms overt umbilical cord prolapse.
This event commonly follows amniotomy when the presenting part is not well applied to the cervix; fetal hypoxia results from cord compression.
Diagnosis is clinical and must not be delayed for imaging: assess fetal heart rate continuously while preparing immediate delivery.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Umbilical cord prolapse.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Placental abruption without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fetal heart rate drop to 70 bpm.
management_principles: Call the obstetric emergency immediately and expedite cesarean delivery unless vaginal birth is clearly imminent and safer.
Relieve cord compression by manually elevating the presenting part and positioning the patient knee-chest or head-down lateral; bladder filling can be used if transfer is prolonged.
Avoid manipulating the cord; if it is exteriorized, cover it loosely with warm saline-soaked gauze and continue continuous fetal monitoring.
Do not delay delivery for further evaluation; consider tocolysis only when it does not delay definitive delivery and according to local protocol.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency: sudden severe prolonged fetal heart rate bradycardia immediately following artificial rupture of membranes. 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks experiencing abrupt fetal bradycardia down to 70 bpm after amniotomy where vaginal examination palpates a pulsating loop of umbilical cord protruding through the cervix requiring elevation of fetal presenting part and immediate STAT Cesarean delivery.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Cord Prolapse Acute Obstetric Emergency.
reference_soap.assessment: Overt umbilical cord prolapse after amniotomy causing acute fetal bradycardia.
reference_soap.plan: Call the obstetric emergency and proceed to immediate cesarean delivery. Continuously elevate the presenting part manually; place the patient in knee-chest or steep head-down lateral position and consider bladder filling to relieve compression. Avoid handling the cord, keep it warm and moist if exteriorized, continue fetal monitoring, and do not delay delivery for further evaluation.

teaching.one_liner: 28F G1P0 at 39 weeks with sudden severe fetal bradycardia after amniotomy and a palpable pulsating cord on exam.
red_flags: Fetal heart rate drop to 70 bpm

must_ask.objective: Explain the emergency and next steps
must_ask.say: The umbilical cord has slipped down ahead of the baby — we need to move to an emergency C-section right now.

must_ask.objective: Instruct positioning to relieve cord compression
must_ask.say: I need you to get on your hands and knees right now to take pressure off the cord.

must_ask.objective: Reassure about manual elevation of presenting part
must_ask.say: I'm going to keep my hand in place to hold the baby's head off the cord until we reach the operating room.

must_ask.objective: Ask about time since rupture of membranes
must_ask.say: When exactly did your water break?

must_ask.objective: Reassure the patient amid the emergency
must_ask.say: I know this is frightening, but we are moving quickly to protect your baby.
